title: Plant diversity accelerates soil carbon release through faster and more diverse root strategies
content:
Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog.


Abstract

Global soil-to-atmosphere carbon (C) fluxes are increasing, yet hopes rest on biodiversity to promote soil C sequestration. While previous experiments show that plant diversity increases biomass production and soil C inputs, its net effect on C sequestration remains unclear because high-diversity communities may also stimulate soil C release. Here, we conducted a biodiversity experiment using 12 native grassland species from three functional groups (grasses, legumes and forbs), assembled in 37 species compositions spanning richness levels of 1, 2, 4, 8 and 12 species. Each composition was represented across 12 blocks (n = 444 planted pots). We measured species-specific fine-root traits and indicators of soil C cycling, including C and N mineralization, microbial biomass and extracellular enzyme activities. Increasing species richness was associated with higher C mineralization and a higher multivariate soil C-release index. Communities shifted towards faster resource-acquisition strategies, indicated by higher community-weighted mean root N concentration and lower root tissue density, and towards greater root functional diversity. The soil C-release index was associated with the fast–slow trait axis and with functional diversity, but not with root diameter or specific root length. A combined model of community-weighted means and functional diversity accounted for 78.4% of variation in the soil C-release index. These findings identify a short-term, trait-associated pathway through which plant diversity can increase potential soil C release. This pathway should be considered alongside diversity-driven increases in plant C inputs, while its consequences for long-term soil C stocks require confirmation in field experiments.
